choices.text: It chose to grow longer legs because it wanted to run faster
Its features developed over many, many generations, not by choice
It can grow a new feature whenever it needs one

questions.feedback: That trap answer is the one to unlearn: An animal can decide to grow a new feature when it needs one. Reteach point: These features did not appear overnight: they developed over many, many generations, not by choice. Check scene s1: the cactus's thorns and thick stem fit the desert so well that they look chosen on purpose, but no living thing chooses its features.
questions.misconception: An animal can decide to grow a new feature when it needs one.
questions.prompt: A pupil says an animal grew a helpful feature because it decided it needed one. What should they say instead?

questions.answer: It is camouflage: the wings match the bark colour, so the moth blends in and hungry birds cannot spot it.
questions.feedback: Scene s2 fixes the idea: blending in keeps animals safe - the moth matches its home, so the bird flies right past without seeing it.
questions.prompt: In one sentence, say why a moth whose wings match the tree bark is hard for a bird to spot.

choices.text: They stay and wait, because winter food is easy to find
They fly thousands of kilometres to warmer places until spring
They grow thick feathers on purpose for the winter

questions.feedback: Scene s3 fixes the journey: birds travel far to survive - they migrate south for winter and return when spring brings food back.
questions.prompt: What do migrating birds do when winter makes food hard to find?

questions.answer: They lose their food and shelter, because the trees that were their home are gone.
questions.feedback: Scene s4 fixes the ending: people change animal homes - clearing a forest takes away the animals' food and shelter, so they must move away.
questions.prompt: In one sentence, say what happens to forest animals when people clear the trees.
